title: Onboarding email that matches the product
metaTitle: Onboarding email that matches the app
excerpt: The email after signup should sound like the interface and point at one next action. A sequence of five tips is a second product they did not ask to learn.
alt: A glass-walled office corridor with a sofa, a floor lamp, and black pendant lights, a clear passage for an article about one next step after signup.
caption: A corridor with a single way forward. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should the first email after signup say?
faqs.answer: Repeat the job they just started, in the same words as the button they pressed, and give one link back to that job. Say what will happen if they do nothing. Skip the company story. They already decided to try the product, and the inbox is a bad place to renegotiate the brand.

faqs.question: How many onboarding emails should you send?
faqs.answer: Send another note only when there is a new, real next action, such as a prerequisite they skipped or a result that is ready. A fixed series of five tips fires whether or not they have done step one. That series teaches people to archive you. Stop when the job is done, or when they have gone quiet and a single plain check-in is more honest.

faqs.question: Should the email match the interface exactly?
faqs.answer: It should use the same names, the same tone, and the same primary action. It does not need the same layout as the app. A short letter with one link is easier to read than a miniature of the dashboard. If the button in the product says Create project, the email should not say Launch your workspace.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
Onboarding email design is the art of sounding like the product in a place the product does not control. The note after signup should use the interface's words and point at one next action. A welcome sequence of five tips is a second product, and they did not agree to take a class.

Write the email as a continuation of the button they just pressed. If the button said "Create project," the subject line should be about the project, not about your founder's journey.

## One action, the same words

Open with the job, not the gratitude essay. "Your workspace is ready. Add the first client to see the Friday view." The link goes to that screen, not to the marketing homepage, and not to a login wall that forgets where they were going. If they must sign in again, return them to the action. A link that dumps them on a dashboard of empty cards wastes the sentence you just spent.

Use the product's nouns. A mismatch here is how people search the interface for a word that only exists in the email. You renamed nothing on purpose, and they still feel lost. Keep a list of the words the empty state, the button, and the email are allowed to share. Three surfaces, one verb.

[Google's people-first guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) is written for pages, and the test still fits a message: does this have a purpose for the person who opened it, and can they tell who sent it. The purpose is the next step. The sender is the product they just touched, with a real reply path if a human should receive the answer. A no-reply address plus a cheerful tour is a flyer.

Say how long the action takes if you know. "About two minutes" is a kindness. "Unlock your potential" is a delay. [Nielsen Norman Group](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) found that people give a page only a short chance to prove its value, often leaving within 10 to 20 seconds unless the point is clear in about 10. An email is skimmed even faster. The first two lines have to carry the action. The rest can be a single detail, then stop.

## What the sequence is allowed to be

Send the next note when there is a new fact. They created the project and have not invited anyone, and invites matter for this product. The report they asked for is ready. A prerequisite is still missing, and the screen will fail without it. Each of those is a reason to write. The calendar is not a reason.

If you do send a short series, each message should be skippable and still true. Message two must not assume they finished message one if your data says they did not. Branch on the state of the account. A tip about advanced filters, sent to someone who has not created the first object, is how you teach them the product is not paying attention.

Stop when the job is underway. A person who has done the core action does not need a drip of basics. Move them to the quieter stream: incidents, if you must, and the occasional note when something they use has changed. The changelog can hold the record. The inbox should not retell it as enthusiasm.

Give every message one link that matters. Secondary links in the footer, for the address and the unsubscribe, are required manners. A row of equal feature buttons is another homepage. They are on a phone. They will tap the wrong one, or none.

## Sound like the interface

Read the email next to the empty state. Same heading energy. Same refusal of hype. If the product is plain and specific, the email cannot suddenly become a launch party. If the product is dense because the work is dense, the email can still be short. Density in the tool is not a license to write a memo.

Trade Moai and Got Next are public examples of interfaces with a point of view. An email for a product like that would name the next control, not the feeling of using it. Borrow the discipline, not the layout. You are writing a letter that points at a screen.

Include the detail that prevents a mistake. "Use the same email you signed up with." "The import expects a header row." One caveat beats a perfect tone. Put the caveat before the link if ignoring it would waste their click. Put it after if it is only a nicety.

Sign it with a name if a human will read replies, or with the product if nobody will. Do not sign with a first name that is a costume. People write back to onboarding mail more often than teams expect. The reply is a research channel. A black hole is a choice you should make on purpose, and then you should not ask them to "just hit reply."

## The practical shape of the letter

A shape you can repeat:

1. Subject line with the object and the verb, not a teaser.
2. Two sentences: where they are, what to do next.
3. One link or button with the same verb as the product.
4. One caveat or expectation, if you have one.
5. A human close, and a way to stop the mail.

Preview text should continue the subject, not repeat it and not pivot to a discount. Many people decide from the preview alone. "Add your first client. Takes about two minutes." is a complete decision. "We saved you a seat" is a costume, unless you literally did.

Plain text matters. A heavy template that breaks in one client, with the action trapped in an image, fails the person who needed it. Put the link in text. Let the template be quiet. Type that looks like the product is enough brand. A second illustration style in the inbox is how the seam from the marketing site sneaks back.

Time the send to the action, not to a batch at 9:00. If they signed up at 16:40, the note should be waiting when they look, not the next morning after they have forgotten the button. Transactional mail that is actually about their account can move faster than a newsletter. Do not mix the two streams. A password-reset neighbor should not also be selling a webinar.

## What to measure

Measure whether they did the action the email named, not whether they opened it. Opens are a weak compliment. The action is the point. If opens are high and the action is rare, the letter promised a different job than the link delivered, or the screen on the other side is the problem. Fix the screen. Do not add another email to compensate.

Read the replies. The words people use when they are confused are the next subject line. If they ask "where do I find clients," your noun is wrong or the link missed. If they ask to be removed, your sequence is longer than their patience, or it continued after they were done. Both are design bugs.

Watch unsubscribe and spam. A burst after message three means message three is the one that felt like a campaign. Cut it, or make it depend on a state that justifies it. A product that nags a finished user is spending the trust the interface just earned.

Keep a single owner for the words, shared with the person who writes empty states. When the button changes, the email changes in the same release. Put both strings in the checklist. A renamed button with an old email is a small incident you caused on purpose.

## Legal, quiet, and still human

Include the postal facts and the unsubscribe your jurisdiction and your sender reputation require. Do it in the footer, in readable type, without a puzzle. A tiny grey line that cannot be tapped is not a courtesy. It is a dare. The same care you give a form label belongs here.

Do not bury a consent change in an onboarding tip. If you need permission for a new use of their data, that is its own clear note, not a postscript under a feature highlight. People skim. A surprise in the footer is how trust leaves without a ticket.

If they have not acted in a while, one plain check-in is enough. "You started a workspace on Tuesday and the first client is still empty. Want the link again, or should we stop these notes?" That sentence respects them. A fake countdown does not. You do not need urgency. You need a door they can close.

On a Hanabi project, these notes are part of the interface design. The studio writes the screen and the sentence that points back to it, so the inbox does not get delegated to a tool's default sequence. The stack can send the mail. The judgment stays with the people who named the button.

## The limit of email

Email cannot finish a confusing product. If the screen is vague, a clearer letter only delivers people to the vagueness faster. Fix the empty state first. Then let the letter point at it. The order matters. Teams that start in the marketing automation tool end up with a curriculum instead of a next step.

Email also cannot be the only help. A person who searches the docs should find the same job, with the same words. Link to that doc if the action needs more than two sentences. Do not paste the entire doc into the message. The message is the door. The doc is the room.

Some users will never open the mail. The product still has to make the next step obvious when they return on their own. The email is a reinforcement, not the only teacher. Design the screen as if the inbox failed, because sometimes it will, and they will still be your user.

The relationship behind these choices, whether you are a partner thinking about the whole path or a vendor filling a template, is the next decision. [A design partner versus a vendor](/blog/a-design-partner-versus-a-vendor) is about saying which one you are before the work starts. Read it if the emails, the empty states, and the site are being produced by people who do not share a sentence.

If you want the product, the empty state, and the first email to sound like one company, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). Bring the latest note and the screen it links to. The gap between them is the brief.
